tablehtml:
Grade

Global assessment

Criteria

1

Well differentiated

Tumour cells resemble mature hepatocytes with minimal to mild atypia

Hepatocellular adenoma or dysplastic nodule may have to be distinguished

Cytoplasm: ranges from abundant and eosinophilic to moderate and basophilic

Nuclei: minimal to mild nuclear atypia

2

Moderately

differentiated

Clearly malignant on H&E staining; morphology strongly suggests hepatocellular differentiation

Cytoplasm: ranges from abundant and eosinophilic to moderate and basophilic

Nuclei: moderate nuclear atypia; occasional multinucleated tumour cells are acceptable

3

Poorly differentiated

Clearly malignant on H&E staining; morphology overlaps with a broad spectrum of poorly differentiated carcinomas

Cytoplasm: ranges from moderate to scant, usually basophilic

Nuclei: marked nuclear pleomorphism, may include anaplastic giant cells

Note: In grade 1, the diagnosis often requires immunohistochemical stains to establish malignancy (see text for details); cytology and morphology require distinction from hepatic adenoma in a non-cirrhotic liver and from a large regenerative nodule or dysplastic nodule in a cirrhotic liver. In grade 3, immunostaining (often a panel) may be required to confirm hepatocytic differentiation. Sarcomatoid and anaplastic morphology is classified as grade 3.

legend: Irregular tumours clusters and trabeculae with abundant intratumoral fibrosis.
The tumour is composed of well-differentiated neoplastic cells with fatty change.
There are focal areas of reticulin loss within the tumor.

The lesion has a predominantly trabecular growth pattern (micro- and macro-trabeculae). The tumor cells are arranged in clusters, of various appearances and sizes, bordered by endothelial cells that are also well recognizable on H/E. The tumor shows a frank infiltrative attitude involving the perilesional capsule and aspects of angioinvasion.

diagnosis: Hepatocellular carcinoma NOS, G2 with overt VETC.
legend: This WSI shows the same case as previously illustrated, stained with immunohistochemistry for CD34. Endothelial cells, immunoreactive for CD34, arrange themselves around the neoplastic tokens, taking on the characteristic appearance of vessels encapsulating tumor clusters (VETC). Note how these clusters can take on an elongated appearance (tumor fragment at the bottom, right part of the section) or a rounded appearance (tumor fragment at the top, left part of the section). Also note how the areas of angioinvasion (tumor fragment at the bottom, central part of the section) appear to be continuous with the main part of the tumor.
Immunostain for CK19 reveals cytoplasmic expression in some tumor cells.
Steatohepatitic subtype. The tumour cells contain fat, and there is intratumoural inflammation and fibrosis.
Clear cell subtype. The abundant clear cytoplasm results from glycogen accumulation.

Chromophobe subtype. The tumour cells have a distinctive cytoplasm that can superficially resemble that of clear cell carcinoma. The nuclei are uniform in the background, with scattered single tumour cells and clusters of tumour cells with striking anaplasia.
The tumour cells have abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli. A pale body is also present.
There is abundant intratumoural lamellated fibrosis.
E Lymphocyte-rich subtype. The tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes outnumber the tumour cells.
Scirrhous subtype. There is dense intratumoural fibrosis.
Macrotrabecular growth pattern. The tumour trabeculae are > 10 cells in thickness.
Hyaline bodies; large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions are present.
Nodule-in-nodule pattern; well-differentiated steatohepatitic hepatocellular carcinoma (at left) with an inner nodule of moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma (at right).
C Moderately differentiated. The tumour cells are clearly malignant but also show hepatic differentiation.
D Poorly differentiated. The tumour shows marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, and an increased N:C ratio.
Small-cell change. The hepatocytes in the centre of the image show small-cell change with increased N:C ratio; a few cells with large-cell change are also present.

A Separate nodules of HCC can represent independent primaries. In cirrhotic livers, they can show a nodule-in-nodule pattern when arising within a high-grade dysplastic nodule (arrow). They are often in different Couinaud segments. B Separate nodules of HCC can also represent intrahepatic metastasis, usually by spread through the portal veins. This pattern typically shows a dominant nodule with smaller satellite nodules (typically < 5) closely approximated to the dominant nodule. T1, T2, T3 represent multiple tumours of different sizes according to the TNM classification.
Large-cell change. Scattered hepatocytes show nuclear hyperchromasia and multinucleation, but a normal N:C ratio is retained.
Low-grade dysplastic nodule. Patchy large-cell change is present.
High-grade dysplastic nodule. Small-cell change can be seen.
A The tumour is well differentiated and difficult to distinguish from a dysplastic nodule on H&E staining.
